newsitem.title: INDIA: Two years on, no news of Kashmir hostages.
newsitem.headline: Two years on, no news of Kashmir hostages.

text.p: Two years after four Western tourists were kidnapped in a picturesque Himalayan valley, their fate remains an enigma even to shepherds who roam the mountainous reaches where guerrillas seized the men.
"They can be dead or they can be alive. In such dense forests, they can hide tourists for years without being noticed," Jameel Ahmad said earlier this week.
Jameel, 50, is the head of a shepherd family that moves between the Kashmir and Jammu regions, across the towering Pirpanjal mountains, in rhythm with the seasons.

On July 4, 1995, Americans Donald Hutchings and John Childs and Britons Paul Wells and Keith Mangan were kidnapped by Al-Faran separatist militants while trekking in Lidderwat, six km (four miles) uphill from their base camp in Aru village.

Four days later, Childs snuck away to safety in a pine forest. On the same day, the angry captors abducted German Dirk Hasert and Norwegian Hans Christian Ostroe. Ostroe was beheaded five weeks later.

Al-Faran, unknown before the kidnappings, demanded the release of jailed separatists in exchange for the hostages. Indian officials, backed by the foreign governments whose nationals were held hostage, refused to bow to the demands.
Talks over the telephone and wireless radio broke down in November 1995.

From time to time Kashmiris report having seen the bearded hostages being led by armed guerrillas. But no sightings have been confirmed, and no one has come forward to collect a one million rupee ($28,000) reward which Jammu and Kashmir state has offered for information about the captive tourists.
"I, along with my friends, tried to know the whereabouts of the tourists," local trekking guide Bashir Ahmad Wani said. "We went deep into the forests, but no clues."
Jammu and Kashmir police chief Gurbachan Jagat told Reuters: "There is no solid information about the hostages but the last confirmed sighting was in November 1995."
"It is unlikely they are alive," a Western diplomat said, "but how can we be sure without seeing their bodies?"
Some of the hostages' relatives have come to Kashmir for the two-year anniversary of the kidnapping and to appeal for news about the men.

"We want an answer to whether our husbands are still alive," Jane Schelly, wife of U.S. hostage Donald Hutchings, told Reuters last week. "We want some clarity, we want some finality, we want some closure."
"Are they dead or are they alive?" asked Birgit Hasert, German hostage Dirk Hasert's sister. "It is very hard, but we can't give up."

Two captured militants have told interrogators that they believe the hostages were shot dead in December 1995 and buried in a forest. Indian authorities, backed by agents from the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation and Scotland Yard, have scoured the area but come up with no clues.
Villagers say they are as puzzled as the families and pray for the return of the men.

"The kidnappings have brought the wrath of God to this village," said Gulam Mohideen Malik, head of Aru village, population 600. "Since July 1995, this village has been without electricity, transport, doctors or school."

After the abductions, authorities banned the entry of foreign tourists into Pahalgam, 12 km (seven miles) downhill from Aru, which is nestled in a pine forest at 3,650 metres (11,970 feet) and a famous base camp for trekking.
"Not a single tourist has visited since July 1995," Aru's chief priest Gulam Nabi said.
"We are praying for good news so that peace and prosperity returns to the village," Malik said.

Pakistan controls one third of the divided Himalayan region and stakes a claim over the rest, which is under Indian rule. Islamabad denies India's claim that it arms and trains militants who cross into Kashmir to fight for independence or a merger with Pakistan.
Kashmir's leading separatist group, the All Parties Hurriyat (Freedom) Conference, says more than 50,000 people have died in insurgency-related violence since 1990.
